stories.title: Migrating the GitHub Copilot runtime to Rust, using Copilot
stories.snippet: A rewrite this size wasn't affordable before agents. Here's what porting the Copilot agent runtime to 800,000 lines of production Rust actually took. The post Migrating the GitHub Copilot runtime to Rust, using Copilot appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
stories.summary: GitHub migrated the Copilot agent runtime from TypeScript on Node.js to Rust, resulting in over 800,000 lines of production Rust code shipped through 128 pull requests, with AI agents writing most of the code. The work was completed primarily by a single developer over a few months, an effort that would have previously taken a whole team a year or two, while the rest of the team continued expanding the runtime's capabilities. The original architecture forced SDK users across six languages to spawn the CLI as a subprocess via JSON-RPC, incurring roughly 100 MB of V8 overhead per client, slow startup, and out-of-process communication for every function call. Rust was chosen because it supports clean in-process embedding through a C ABI, minimal dependencies, low startup and memory overhead, predictable resource use, and strong foreign function interface support for C#, TypeScript, Python, Go, and Java SDKs. Approximately 430,000 lines of TypeScript passed through the port, and the resulting runtime delivered orders-of-magnitude performance improvements.

stories.title: Grit your teeth and ship it
stories.summary: A tension exists between producing high-quality work and actually shipping it, as Ira Glass observed when he noted that creative people have good taste but often find their early work disappointing. In programming, gifted developers with a strong desire for elegant, correct systems often struggle to ship because flaws in their code bother them emotionally, which can be fatal at tech companies where compromise with existing codebases is necessary. Some gifted programmers freeze up, retreat to safer tasks like refactoring tests, or quit entirely. Drawing on personal experience writing blog posts, the author notes that posts felt poorly written often resonated with audiences while posts considered strong went unnoticed. Since creators cannot predict which work will succeed, producing high volume yields better results than polishing a few pieces, making it essential to prioritize momentum and consistently force oneself to ship.

stories.title: Should you read the code, is RAG dead, and did Skills kill MCP?
stories.snippet: We dive into these questions and other AI hot takes on the latest episode of the GitHub Podcast. The post Should you read the code, is RAG dead, and did Skills kill MCP? appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
stories.summary: The GitHub Podcast explores five AI hot takes, pushing back against oversimplified claims. While developers remain responsible for AI-generated code, review intensity should match the risk rather than treating every change identically. Hiring now values AI judgment and the ability to explain when and how you use tools, not total adoption or refusal. Skills haven't killed MCP because the two serve different roles: MCP provides standardized tool access while skills deliver project-specific context and best practices. RAG also remains relevant, grounding models in external information like documentation and codebases to reduce wasted tokens and improve accuracy. If a model can't make sense of a codebase, that likely signals maintainability problems, and projects like Pollinations AI and Avian Visitors show how building creates more value than debating.

stories.title: Marketing ops as code: Automating events from planning to follow-up on GitHub
stories.snippet: If you can write down how you do your work, you can automate it. Here's what I did to support GitHub's APAC marketing team. The post Marketing ops as code: Automating events from planning to follow-up on GitHub appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
stories.summary: Tomoko Tanaka, who runs marketing for GitHub in Japan and Korea, automated her APAC event workflow using GitHub's native tools, starting from a runbook file called AGENTS.md that guides GitHub Copilot through event planning conversations. Each event becomes a GitHub Issue created from structured forms, with labels acting as triggers for GitHub Actions workflows that duplicate landing pages, generate UTM-tagged URLs, produce invitation emails, file request issues, and update project boards. A DRY_RUN repository variable lets the team rehearse every workflow without touching external systems, while a daily cron job screens registrants and waitlists against defined criteria. Post-event follow-up runs through slash commands like /lead-upload and /event-report, each backed by a SKILL.md file written in prose. The whole system depends on the event platform's API and the CRM's CLI, and Tanaka argues that any marketer whose tools offer a scriptable entry point can apply the same pattern.

stories.summary: FAMOS is a feed-forward model designed to predict movable-part segmentation and joint parameters from a sparse, unordered set of partial point clouds of articulated objects. Unlike prior feed-forward methods that infer articulation from a single observation and depend heavily on category-level shape priors, FAMOS aggregates cues across multiple views while still supporting a variable number of inputs, including single-view cases. At its core is a Multi-state Articulation Transformer that uses alternating state-wise and global attention to combine articulation evidence across observations. The model is trained with an observed articulation span objective that supervises the motion range each part exhibits across the input set, encouraging use of all available observations. To address limited training data, the authors introduce a procedural data generator that synthesizes self-annotated assets during training. Experiments on PartNet-Mobility, ACD, and ArtiCraft-10K demonstrate consistent improvements over both feed-forward and optimization-based baselines.

stories.title: Workspace Models: Lightweight Robotic Memory via Saliency-Driven Supervision
stories.snippet: Complex robotic manipulation tasks frequently require a long-term memory of past events and actions. As conditioning on full histories renders policies prone to spurious correlations and degrades performance, many approaches to policy memory involve compressing historical information through expensive VLM queries in-the-loop to process only task-salient information. In this paper, we propose an alternative approach in which computationally intensive VLM queries are made during train-time to learn a lightweight latent memory that can be efficiently queried at deployment time. Our representation, which we call the \textbf{workspace token}, is trained by (1) using a VLM to identify current and historical information necessary for completing a task, then (2) distilling these into the workspace
stories.summary: Complex robotic manipulation tasks often require long-term memory of past events, but conditioning policies on full histories can introduce spurious correlations and degrade performance. Existing approaches instead rely on expensive vision-language model queries in-the-loop to process only task-salient information. The authors propose moving these computationally intensive VLM queries to training time in order to learn a compact latent memory they call the workspace token. Training proceeds in two stages: a VLM first identifies which current and historical information is needed for the task, and this supervision is then distilled into the workspace token using a set-reconstruction decoder loss. At deployment, the workspace token acts as a drop-in replacement for raw observations, enabling policies to solve memory-intensive tasks without in-the-loop VLM reasoning. Experiments in both simulation and hardware show that workspace tokens are not only more lightweight but also lead to better policy performance than existing alternatives.

stories.title: Coding Agents with an Obstacle-Aware Harness for Safe Robot Manipulation
stories.snippet: Coding agents have emerged as a promising paradigm for robot manipulation: a language model writes the robot controller as a program, and agents built in this way now operate robots without robot-specific training.Whether this paradigm is also safe, however, has not been asked. We evaluate coding agent under a safety constraint, where each task pairs a manipulation goal with an obstacle the robot must not touch. The agent pursues the goal but collides with the obstacle in most cases, treating task completion as its sole objective while neglecting safety. The agent reasons about the obstacle in its traces, and the prompt already forbids touching it, so neither perception nor instruction is at fault; the fault lies in the planning, where the stated constraint never becomes a priority. stories.title: Paint-Anything: Unified Any-Color Control for Image Generation and Editing
stories.snippet: Professional design requires any-color control: the ability to specify an object's target color with any 24-bit hex value for image generation and editing. Prior work has explored color generation, editing, and colorization, but often relies on dedicated color representations or specialized inference procedures. Advances in large language models offer a simpler starting point: even compact models can associate hex values with color semantics. We present Paint-Anything, which learns a shared hex-prompt interface for generation and editing through object-level color supervision. We develop a data pipeline that constructs Paint-500K from real images through object grounding, perceptual color labeling, and editing-pair synthesis. Since shadows make real-image labels only approximate colors, we
stories.summary: Paint-Anything is a method that enables any-color control for image generation and editing by letting users specify target object colors using 24-bit hex values. Unlike prior work that relies on dedicated color representations or specialized inference procedures, it learns a shared hex-prompt interface for both tasks through object-level color supervision. The authors build Paint-500K, a dataset constructed from real images using object grounding, perceptual color labeling, and editing-pair synthesis. To address noise from shadows in real-image labels, they complement supervision with pure-color anchors that exactly match their paired hex values, applied only at high-noise timesteps while low-noise training uses natural images. They also introduce Any Color Benchmark (ACBench), containing ACBench-T2I and ACBench-Edit for evaluating object-level hex color fidelity. Tested on FLUX.2-4B, Paint-Anything improves ACBench-T2I and ACBench-Edit scores by 85.3% and 28.3% over the base model and achieves the highest average CompColor score among compared methods.

stories.title: ERCPMP-Gx: Endoscopic Image and Video Dataset for Morphological, Histopathological, and Genomic Characterization of Colorectal Polyposis
stories.snippet: Hereditary polyposis syndromes can be precursor lesions to colorectal cancer and are associated with a broad spectrum of extracolonic tumors. Early identification and accurate classification of these syndromes are essential for timely diagnosis, individualized patient management, and targeted surveillance strategies for affected families. However, public endoscopic datasets are largely organized around the individual sporadic polyp, and none links the polyposis phenotype to histopathology and germline findings at the patient level. Here, we present ERCPMP-Gx, an endoscopic, histopathological, and genomic dataset developed to support the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in the recognition, characterization, and classification of colorectal polyposis. stories.summary: The ERCPMP-Gx dataset was developed to support artificial intelligence applications in recognizing, characterizing, and classifying colorectal polyposis syndromes, which are precursor lesions to colorectal cancer. It comprises 160 endoscopic images and accompanying video clips, most acquired using the Olympus EVIS X1 system with white-light endoscopy, narrow-band imaging, magnifying NBI, and NBI with near focus modes. Approximately eighty percent of cases represent hereditary polyposis syndromes, including familial adenomatous polyposis, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, juvenile polyposis syndrome, and ganglioneuroma syndrome, while the remaining twenty percent consist of non-hereditary polyps and polyp-mimicking lesions included for differential classification. Each released record is linked to standardized endoscopic annotations, representative histopathology, and clinically reported germline findings, forming an AI-ready patient-level annotation framework. The dataset is publicly available on Mendeley, addressing a gap left by existing public endoscopic datasets that focus on individual sporadic polyps rather than linking the polyposis phenotype to histopathology and germline findings at the patient level.

stories.title: We made Playwright 2x faster and 80% more token efficient
stories.summary: Stagehand is an SDK for extracting data and interacting with websites, built specifically for AI agents and available in TypeScript, Python, and Go. It claims to be 2x faster and 80% more token efficient than Playwright, using hybrid accessibility-tree trimming to provide agents with only the page context they need. The SDK runs as an extension next to the browser, reducing round-trip latency, and offers self-healing act, observe, and extract commands that adapt when sites change. The observe method returns real CSS selectors so sensitive input like credentials never reaches the model, while extract returns schema-validated data. Stagehand can run locally or on the Browserbase cloud platform, which adds a Model Gateway that automatically selects the cheapest model per action and server-side caching for repeated calls. It also exposes an MCP server for coding agents and offers Search and Fetch tools for lightweight web access without a browser.

stories.title: Show HN: CUA-S1 – A System One Model for Computer Use
stories.snippet: Hello HN! We're Dillon and Francesco from Cua. We were wondering how many computer use tasks actually need a full general purpose LLM (e.g. gpt-6-astra, claude-opus-5 etc.) to think through all their decisions and steps. Some tasks require thinking about a plan, exploring different paths, recovering from failure. Other tasks are a question of making local decisions, like this value should go in this box, or should I check this box, or this element should be ignored. We wondered how far we could go with a small model trained to only make these kinds of decisions. Our inspiration was Typesafe's Jev and its System One Model framing. This is a nod to the dichotomy between thinking quickly, automatically, and intuitively (system 1) vs. thinking slowly, analytically (system 2), as desc
stories.summary: Cua is an open-source platform that gives AI agents computers they can use, providing isolated cloud desktops, local macOS virtual machines, specialist decision models, and benchmarks for evaluating computer-use agents. The platform includes Cua Fleets for provisioning Linux cloud desktops and running commands, Cua Driver for operating native desktop apps and browsers across macOS, Windows, and Linux, and Lume for creating local macOS and Linux VMs on Apple Silicon. CUA-S1 is a family of small, specialized System 1 models designed for fast, bounded decisions, with the first research profile focusing on form-scoring decisions rather than generating response tokens. Cua Bench enables users to build and evaluate computer-use tasks, including simulated tasks that require no virtual machine or model API key. The project is hosted on GitHub under an MIT license, with CUA-S1 model weights hosted separately on Hugging Face.

stories.title: Show HN: An e-ink frame that hears birds and draws them as 1800s illustrations
stories.snippet: See also: Avian Visitors - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48343424 - May 2026 (20 comments)
stories.summary: Fugleramme is an e-ink bird frame for Raspberry Pi that detects birds by audio using BirdNET-Go and renders them as hand-cut 1800s natural-history illustrations. The project, currently running from a kitchen window in Bergen, Norway, pairs a Raspberry Pi 5 with an Inky Impression 13.3" e-ink panel and matches over 400 species to more than 800 curated public-domain cut

stories.title: Show HN: I created an open source locally usable full fledged AI platform
stories.snippet: hi to all the readers this post is for my recent opensource project called ENZO now answering what is enzo so enzo is an opensource platform where i clubbed all the free available api for anyone use under one hood with more than 2000 models available to use for chatting coding researching and much more now answering the most common question of why you should put your time looking the project so it has few distinct feature meaning it has a dedicated agents tab where you can describe your need and create a special agent just for one specific task with master ability in that domain second it has the ability to connect your gmail drive and calendar and then you can ask it to perform some specific tasks like reading you the most important mail of the day or finding recruiter mails and creating
stories.summary: ENZO is an open source AI platform that can be self-hosted via Docker or run on Google Colab, providing a unified workspace for chatting with 300+ models across 9 providers without accounts, subscriptions, or middleman fees. The platform is built in TypeScript with strict mode across approximately 44,000 lines of code and includes features like an agent builder, deep research mode, code generation, a music player, and a file converter. API keys are sealed in the browser using AES-256-GCM encryption under a non-extractable WebCrypto key, with optional passphrase protection. Security is emphasized through a 44-assertion black-box pentest run on every CI push alongside 298 unit and security tests. The current v1.4.0 release adds in-chat file conversion for PDFs and spreadsheets, Google Colab support, and self-healing Docker dependency checks.

stories.title: I built non-autoregressive decision models with RL a year ago
stories.summary: The author built non-autoregressive decision models with reinforcement learning a year ago, publishing arXiv papers (2503.23303 and 2510.01237), open weights, and a dataset, then watched TypeSafe AI launch a similar closed-source product called Jev in September 2026. In response, they created Laya, an open-source Apache 2.0 family of bidirectional encoder models that output probabilities directly through three primitives: choice, score, and noul. Laya includes three specialized checkpoints bundled in a single Hugging Face repository, with a sub-millisecond router that detects Unicode scripts to dispatch text to the appropriate model, since English tokenizers catastrophically fail on non-Latin scripts while reporting high confidence. The model runs in 32.8 ms on a single GPU, is 6–8x faster than Jev, supports 100+ languages, and outperforms Jev on benchmarks like typed-decisions (0.766 vs 0.727) and DAIR Emotion (0.595 vs 0.480) at zero API cost. However, the author acknowledges that choice questions degrade beyond 20 options, scoring only 0.425 on Banking77's 77-label task compared to Jev's 0.870.

stories.title: Cloudflare Quick Tunnels
stories.summary: Cloudflare Quick Tunnels transform a locally running server into a public, encrypted URL hosted on Cloudflare's edge with a single command, requiring no account, DNS configuration, or open ports. The cloudflared tool establishes an outbound-only connection to the nearest edge location, allowing traffic to the tunnel URL to travel through Cloudflare's network back to the user's machine. Setup takes about three seconds with no sign-up, config file, or DNS waiting, and the URL is generated almost immediately. Every tunnel comes with automatic HTTPS, DDoS filtering, and certificate management, routing traffic through any of Cloudflare's 335+ edge cities. The feature now includes JSON output designed for coding agents and supports any web server, port, or stack, making it suitable for previews, CI, webhooks, and evaluation harnesses.

stories.title: AI-generated posters don’t have to be horrible
stories.summary: AI-generated posters often share a repetitive, easily-recognizable style that has become irritating through overuse. The author tested ChatGPT by providing invented event details for a spring fayre and requesting specific design aesthetics instead of the default look. Requesting particular styles—including Bauhaus/Modernist, Stamp/Letterpress, Japanese Minimal, Memphis Design, Designers Republic, a child's painting with professional typography, 1980s punk fanzine, 90s drum and bass flyers, and a 1940s cubist exhibition poster—produced distinctive results that stand apart from typical identikit village fayre posters. While the AI-generated nature remains detectable, the varied approaches yielded designs that are visually interesting rather than generic. The author also notes that tools like Claude and Gemini can generate editable formats with real text and layers, and has compiled a catalogue of one hundred poster styles with ready-to-use prompts and examples.
